title: The Great Orange Sunset Machine
spine: We want to paint a giant orange sunset banner for Grandma's porch, but we only have red and yellow paint—so we must invent our way to the perfect orange, one swirl at a time.

segments.text:
Grandpa's garage smells like sawdust and old rain boots. We have newspaper spread everywhere. On the floor. On the table. Even on the cat.

"Today," we say, "we paint a giant orange sunset banner for the porch!"

Grandpa claps. "Splendid!" He squeezes out two fat blobs of paint. One red, one yellow. They sit on the palette like two little hills.

Mixmaster Max watches from the workbench. He is Grandpa's old garden gnome, with a pointy hat covered in dried paint drips. He holds the palette with his stiff plaster hands. He is very good at supervising.

"Now," says Grandpa. "Where is the orange?"

We look. No orange. Only red. Only yellow.

"Hmm," we say. "We need orange."

Max's hat wiggles. Just a tiny bit.

"Careful scientists," we say. "One drop at a time."

Grandpa nods. "Very wise." He squeezes fresh red onto a clean corner of the palette. Then yellow. Two little islands, not touching.

We dip the brush in red. Then yellow. Swirl, swirl, slow.

"Look," we whisper. The red is turning peachy at the edges.

Mixmaster Max leans in. His hat nearly touches the paint. "Steady," says Grandpa.

Swirl. Swirl. The yellow melts into the red like butter into toast.

"Is it orange yet?" we ask.

Max's hat wiggles. Not quite. But something is happening in the middle of the palette, something warm and glowing, like a tiny sun waking up.

"Crazy inventors!" we shout. "Great big swoosh!"

Grandpa grins. "My favorite kind." He hands us the big brush, the one as wide as a spoon.

We plunge it into the red blob. Then the yellow. Swoosh!

Paint flies. A red dot lands on Mixmaster Max's nose. He does not blink. He is very professional.

"Again!" says Grandpa.

Swoosh, swoosh! The colors crash together like waves. Red streaks through yellow. Yellow streaks through red. It looks like a storm on the palette.

"Whoa," we breathe. The middle is glowing. But the edges are wild, all swirly and streaky.

Max's hat tilts. Is it supposed to look like that?

Grandpa leans over the palette. "What did you find?" he asks.

We show him. He nods slowly, the way he does when the tomato soup needs stirring.

"Ah," he says. "A wobble. Every good mix has one."

He holds our brush under the tap. The water runs pink, then clear. "Clean tools," he says, "make true colors."

We dip the brush. We add yellow, bit by bit. The red softens. Tangerine. Then glowing sunset orange.

"Look!" we shout, because we cannot help it.

Mixmaster Max's hat wiggles. The orange swirls on the palette like a tiny sun, right there in Grandpa's garage.

"Now," says Grandpa, "the banner."

We paint the sun with our perfect orange. Big, round strokes. While it dries, a real bee lands on the windowsill. Its legs are dusted yellow, just like our paint. "Look," we whisper. "It carried the yellow here." Grandpa nods. "Then let's give it somewhere to land." We mix a tiny drop of red into white. Pink. Soft as a kitten's ear. We dab a flower in the corner. The bee hums. We hang the banner on the porch. The real sunset matches ours. The bee visits our painted blossom. "Hello Sunshine," we say. Max's hat wiggles.

We paint the sun with our perfect orange. Then we look under the workbench. The shadow there is gray, not orange. "Why?" we ask. Grandpa scratches his chin. "Let's find out." We add one tiny drop of black to our orange. It turns brown, like mud. We paint a cool shadow beneath our sun. "Shadows aren't gray," Grandpa says. "They're where the light hides." We hang the banner on the porch. The real sun sets. Our painted shadow grows long. "Hello Sunshine," we say. Max's hat wiggles.
